entities.name: Caesarius of Arles
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Caesarius of Arles (b. c. 470 CE, Chalon-sur-Saône – d. August 26, 542 CE, Arles) emerged as one of the most influential ecclesiastics of Late Antiquity, an era witnessing the profound transformation of the Roman West into early medieval Europe. As Archbishop of Arles from 502 until his death, he presided over a vital see in Gaul, strategically positioned amidst the shifting powers of Visigoths, Ostrogoths, and Franks. Caesarius dedicated his life to monastic reform, the propagation of orthodox Christian doctrine, and the establishment of ecclesiastical order, significantly shaping the nascent institutional structures of the Western Church.

His tenure as archbishop was marked by tireless pastoral activity, including the composition of over 200 accessible sermons designed for widespread catechesis, and the drafting of monastic rules for both monks and nuns—most notably the *Regula ad monachos* and *Regula ad virgines*. A staunch defender of Augustinian theology, Caesarius played a pivotal role in the condemnation of Semi-Pelagianism, presiding over the Second Council of Orange in 529 CE. This council's decrees, affirming grace as primary in salvation, became a foundational document for Western soteriology. His political acumen was also evident in navigating the complex loyalties required by successive Gothic and Frankish rulers, often enduring exile or imprisonment for his unwavering commitment to his flock.
